title: trataka
hook: a clay lamp on a windowsill lies flat when the door opens, and stands up again when it shuts

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka began: a still gaze at one small mark, until the eyes water. While you were waiting somewhere, did your eyes rest on one point, or did the phone win? Day one thousand twenty-seven.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `A STILL GAZE AT ONE SMALL MARK.`

segments.voice: A small clay lamp sits on a windowsill, a cotton wick in a pool of oil. Someone opens the front door. A draft runs through the house, and the flame lies down sideways, thin and blue, nearly out. The door shuts. For a moment the flame shivers. Then it stands back up, tall and still, as if nothing happened. It is a small drama, easy to miss. The Bhagavad Gita uses that same flame to describe a mind. Yesterday trataka gave the eyes a small mark. Today, the flame that so often becomes that mark, and what the Gita sees in it.
screen: `A CLAY LAMP ON A WINDOWSILL.` → `THE DOOR OPENS. THE FLAME LIES DOWN.` → `THE DOOR SHUTS. IT STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna describes someone sitting in meditation, and then gives a single picture. In paraphrase: as a lamp in a place without wind does not flicker, so is the mind of the yogi who has gathered it in. That's the whole image. A flame, and no wind. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say the yogi has no mind, or that the flame goes out. The lamp is still burning. It's still giving light. What's gone is the flicker. Arjuna, listening, isn't convinced. A few verses later he pushes back, in paraphrase: the mind is restless, Krishna, stubborn and strong, and holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. It's an honest complaint, and the text keeps it in. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees the mind is hard to hold. Then he names two things that hold it: abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go. Practice is coming back, again and again. Letting go is not feeding every draft that blows through. Earlier in the same chapter, Krishna gives the coming back in plain terms: wherever the restless mind wanders off, draw it back from there, and rest it again in the Self. This is why the flame suits trataka so well. When the eyes rest on a flame, they watch the very thing the Gita compares the mind to. When a thought blows through, the flame on the table may stand perfectly still while attention leans sideways. The practice is simply to notice the lean, and come back to the flame. Over and over. The Gita never promises the wind will stop forever. It describes a lamp in a sheltered place, and a person who keeps coming back to it.
screen: `A LAMP WHERE NO WIND BLOWS.` · `ARJUNA: AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.` · `PRACTICE, AND LETTING GO.` · `WHEREVER IT WANDERS, DRAW IT BACK.` · then, large: `THE FLAME STILL BURNS. ONLY THE FLICKER GOES.`

segments.voice: Set a small point in front of you at eye level: a candle flame if you have one safely lit, or a mark on the wall. Sit comfortably and let the eyes rest on it. Blink whenever you need to. Each time a thought pulls you away, a sound, a plan, a memory, notice the lean, like a flame in a draft. Then come back to the point. No scolding, just return. If the eyes tire, close them for a while, then open them and look again. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, with the Gita's lamp in a windless place, and the coming back each time the mind leans.

Your line: trataka. Today, the next time your attention gets pulled sideways mid-task, notice the lean like a flame in a draft, and bring it back to the one thing in front of you. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Some who practice trataka use a candle or ghee lamp set at eye level in a still, draft-free room, and some recall the Gita's image of a lamp in a windless place as they sit.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: abhyasa, practice, the returning again and again. In the Gita, paired with vairagya, letting go.

trapdoor: what you thought: a still mind is an empty mind.
what it means: in the Gita, it's a lamp still burning, without the flicker.
what a scholar hears: Gita 6.19, the lamp in a windless place, and 6.34–35, abhyasa and vairagya.
